summary.text: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into large plates that have been slowly moving since 3–4 billion years ago.
Where plates meet, their relative motion makes a convergent, divergent or transform boundary, and these zones see earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain-building and ocean trenches.
At subduction zones one plate sinks into the mantle, while new ocean crust forms at spreading ridges, so Earth's total surface area stays constant like a conveyor belt.

facts.label: Major plates
facts.value: Seven or eight, plus many minor platelets

facts.label: Fast mover
facts.value: Nazca plate, about 160 mm per year

facts.label: Accepted by geoscientists
facts.value: After seafloor spreading was validated in the 1960s

items.prompt: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates move apart at roughly the speed of something in your everyday life. What?

options.label: A garden snail crawling
Your fingernails growing
A lawn's grass growing
A slow river flowing

items.explain: Plates at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge move about 10 to 40 millimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.

items.prompt: Most of the seafloor sits below sea level, while continents stand above it. What best explains the difference?

options.label: Ocean water presses the seafloor down
Continents rest on giant hidden pillars
Ocean crust is denser than land crust
Ocean crust is much older than land

items.explain: Oceanic crust has less silicon and more heavier elements, so it is denser and lies below sea level while lighter continental crust rides higher.

items.prompt: Subduction keeps dragging plate edges down into the mantle. Why hasn't Earth's surface shrunk away over billions of years?

options.label: The planet itself keeps slowly growing
Sunken plates bounce back up intact
Meteorites add fresh crust each year
New ocean crust forms at spreading ridges

items.explain: Crust lost at subduction zones is balanced by new oceanic crust made at divergent margins, keeping the total surface area constant.

items.prompt: Several forces have been proposed for what pushes and pulls the plates. Which is considered the strongest driver?

options.label: Cold, dense ocean plate sinking into the mantle
The Moon's tidal pull dragging plates along
Earth's spin flinging plates toward the equator
Sunlight heating and stretching the crust

items.explain: At subduction zones, relatively cold, dense oceanic crust sinks into the mantle, and this is the strongest driver of plate motion; the Moon's tidal drag is still debated.

items.prompt: A research ship sails from a mid-ocean ridge toward a distant subduction zone, measuring the ocean plate beneath it. What does it find?

options.label: The plate gets thicker as it goes
The plate gets thinner as it goes
The plate stays the same thickness
The plate vanishes halfway across

items.explain: Ocean plate cools and adds mantle to its base as it moves away from the ridge, growing from about 6 km thick at the ridge to over 100 km at subduction zones.

items.prompt: You plot every active volcano on Earth on a map of the plates. Where do most of the dots land?

options.label: Spread evenly over the whole globe
Deep in the middle of plates
Clustered near the two poles
Along the edges where plates meet

items.explain: The vast majority of active volcanoes occur along plate boundaries, with the Pacific's Ring of Fire the best known.
